1 — Introduction¶

In this lab, we use nonsmooth convex optimization to estimate how the reproduction number of COVID-19 changes over time.

We start with daily infection data and apply the methods studied in class to obtain reliable estimates. We then explore how regularization affects the results and compare two approaches: L1 and Tikhonov regularization.

Our goal is not only to make the algorithms work, but also to understand their behavior, explain our choices, and discuss what the results tell us.

We denote by $Z_t$ the number of new infections on day $t$ and by $\Phi_t^Z$ the infectiousness estimated from previous observations. We assume a Poisson model: $ Z_t \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(R_t\Phi_t^Z).$

To estimate $R_t$, we minimize the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between observed and predicted infections. We also penalize second-order differences to obtain more stable estimates, using $\ell_1$ and Tikhonov regularization.

2 — Context, model and goals¶

From the very beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic National Health Authorities of all countries worldwide are monitoring the number of new infections each day, denoted by $Z_t$ at day $t$. An example of such daily counts for five weeks in October and November 2022 in France is provided in Figure 1, as collected and make available by Johns Hopkins $University^1$.

c) Show that the function $p_t$ → $d_{KL}$ $(Z_t|p_t)$ is convex and differentiable.

For $z>0$ and $p>0$, the first and second derivatives are

$$ \frac{\partial d_{\mathrm{KL}}(z\mid p)}{\partial p} = 1-\frac{z}{p}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 d_{\mathrm{KL}}(z\mid p)}{\partial p^2} = \frac{z}{p^2}>0. $$

For $z=0$, we have

$$ d_{\mathrm{KL}}(0\mid p)=p, \qquad p\geq 0. $$

Answer 2(c).

For positive z, the second derivative is positive, so the KL divergence is strictly convex and differentiable for p > 0. When z = 0, the function is linear and remains convex and differentiable on the interior of its domain.

d) Is the gradient of $p_t$ → $d_{KL}$ $(Z_t|p_t)$ Lipschitzian? Justify your answer.

For $z>0$, the second derivative is

$$ \frac{\partial^2 d_{\mathrm{KL}}(z\mid p)}{\partial p^2} =\frac{z}{p^2} \xrightarrow[p\to 0^+]{}+\infty. $$

However, for $p\geq\varepsilon>0$, it is bounded by

$$ \left|\frac{\partial^2 d_{\mathrm{KL}}(z\mid p)}{\partial p^2}\right| \leq \frac{z}{\varepsilon^2} =L. $$

Answer 2(d).

For z > 0, the gradient is not globally Lipschitz because the second derivative becomes unbounded near p = 0. It is Lipschitz when p is bounded away from zero; for z = 0, the gradient is constant.

3 — Estimation of the reproduction number¶

3.1 — Maximum Likelihood Estimator

a) Given fixed $Z_t$ and $\Phi_t^Z=\sum_{u=1}^{\tau_\phi}\phi(u)Z_{t-u}$ , compute the minimum and the minimizer of the function $d_{\mathrm{KL}}: R_t \mapsto d_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z_t \mid R_t\Phi_t^Z)$.

For $Z_t>0$ and $\Phi_t^Z>0$, we differentiate the KL divergence with respect to $R_t$:

$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial R_t} d_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z_t\mid R_t\Phi_t^Z) = \Phi_t^Z-\frac{Z_t}{R_t}=0. $$

This gives

$$ \boxed{ R_t^*=\frac{Z_t}{\Phi_t^Z}, \qquad \min_{R_t\geq 0} d_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z_t\mid R_t\Phi_t^Z)=0. } $$

Answer 3.1(a).

The KL divergence is minimized when the predicted number of infections matches the observed count. For Z = 0, the minimum is also zero and is reached at R = 0.

b) Deduce the minimum and the minimizer $\widehat{\mathbf{R}}^{\mathrm{MLE}}$ of the Kullback-Leibler divergence

$$ D_{\mathrm{KL}}: \begin{cases} \mathbb{R}^{T} \to \mathbb{R} \\ \mathbf{R} \mapsto \displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T} d_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z_t \mid R_t\Phi_t^Z) \end{cases} $$

The KL divergence is a sum of independent terms:

$$ D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z\mid R\odot\Phi^Z) = \sum_{t=1}^{T} d_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z_t\mid R_t\Phi_t^Z). $$

Applying the result from Question 3.1(a) to each day gives

$$ \boxed{ \widehat{R}^{\mathrm{MLE}} = Z\oslash\Phi^Z, \qquad \min_{R\geq 0} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z\mid R\odot\Phi^Z)=0. } $$

Answer 3.1(b).

Since the KL divergence is separable, we can estimate the reproduction number independently for each day. Assuming positive infectiousness, the minimum is zero because the predicted infection counts match the observed data.

d) Would you advocate the use of the Maximum Likelihood Estimator to monitor the COVID-19 pandemic? Explain why.

Answer 3.1(d).

The MLE is not reliable enough for epidemic monitoring because it reacts strongly to daily fluctuations in reported cases. Adding temporal regularization can reduce these variations and make transmission trends easier to follow.

3.2 — Penalized likelihood

a) Based on Question 2 d. explain why it is not possible to use the forward-backward algorithm.

Answer 3.2(a).

The standard Forward–Backward algorithm is not suitable because the gradient of the KL divergence is not globally Lipschitz, as shown in Question 2(d). A primal–dual algorithm is more appropriate because it handles both the KL divergence and the nonsmooth regularization through proximal operators.

b) For fixed $Z_t$, compute the proximity operator of $p_t$ → $d_{KL}$ $(Z_t|p_t)$.

For $z>0$, the proximal operator is defined by

$$ \operatorname{prox}_{\gamma d_{\mathrm{KL}}(z\mid\cdot)}(v) = \underset{p>0}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left\{ \frac{1}{2}(p-v)^2 + \gamma d_{\mathrm{KL}}(z\mid p) \right\}. $$

The first-order optimality condition gives

$$ p-v+\gamma\left(1-\frac{z}{p}\right)=0. $$

Solving for $p$ and including the case $z=0$, we obtain

$$ \boxed{ \operatorname{prox}_{\gamma d_{\mathrm{KL}}(z\mid\cdot)}(v) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{v-\gamma+\sqrt{(v-\gamma)^2+4\gamma z}}{2}, & z>0,\\[10pt] \max(v-\gamma,0), & z=0. \end{cases} } $$

Answer 3.2(b).

The optimality condition leads to a quadratic equation, whose positive root gives the proximal operator. When z = 0, the result simplifies to a positive-part threshold.

c) Given $Z_t$ and $\Phi_t^Z=\sum_{u=1}^{\tau_\phi}\phi(u)Z_{t-u}$, deduce from 2.b the expression of the proximity
operator of $R_t \mapsto d_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z_t \mid R_t\Phi_t^Z)$.

Let $f_t(r)=d_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z_t\mid r\Phi_t^Z)$, with $\Phi_t^Z>0$.

The proximal operator is defined by

$$ \operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f_t}(v) = \underset{r\geq 0}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left\{ \frac{1}{2}(r-v)^2 + \gamma d_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z_t\mid r\Phi_t^Z) \right\}. $$

For $Z_t>0$, the optimality condition is

$$ r-v+\gamma\left(\Phi_t^Z-\frac{Z_t}{r}\right)=0. $$

Solving this equation gives

$$ \boxed{ \operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f_t}(v) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{ v-\gamma\Phi_t^Z+ \sqrt{(v-\gamma\Phi_t^Z)^2+4\gamma Z_t} }{2}, & Z_t>0,\\[12pt] \max\left(v-\gamma\Phi_t^Z,0\right), & Z_t=0. \end{cases} } $$

Answer 3.2(c).

The infectiousness term changes the optimality condition but still leads to a quadratic equation. We take its positive root when Z is positive; when Z = 0, the result is a simple threshold.

d) Explain how to compute the proximity operator of $ D_{\mathrm{KL}}: \left\{ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{R}^{T} &\to \mathbb{R},\\ \mathbf{R} &\mapsto \sum_{t=1}^{T} d_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z_t \mid R_t\Phi_t^Z). \end{aligned} \right. $

Let $F(R)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z\mid R\odot\Phi^Z)$.

Since the KL divergence is separable, its proximal operator can be computed independently for each day:

$$ \operatorname{prox}_{\gamma F}(v) = \underset{R\geq 0}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left\{ \frac{1}{2}\|R-v\|_2^2 + \gamma D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z\mid R\odot\Phi^Z) \right\}. $$

Using the result from Question 3.2(c), for $t=1,\ldots,T$,

$$ \boxed{ \left[\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma F}(v)\right]_t = \frac{ v_t-\gamma\Phi_t^Z+ \sqrt{(v_t-\gamma\Phi_t^Z)^2+4\gamma Z_t} }{2}. } $$

For $Z_t=0$, this reduces to

$$ \left[\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma F}(v)\right]_t = \max\left(v_t-\gamma\Phi_t^Z,0\right). $$

Answer 3.2(d).

The KL divergence is separable, so we apply the scalar proximal operator to each day independently. This gives a nonnegative estimate and allows us to compute the full operator efficiently.

e) Compute the proximity operator of the $\ell_1$ norm multiplied by a scalar $\lambda\sigma^{-1}$, that is of

$ \lambda\sigma^{-1}\|\cdot\|_1 : \mathbf{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^N \mapsto \sum_{n=1}^{N}\lambda\sigma^{-1}|Q_n| \in\mathbb{R}, $ and explain how to compute it in practice.

Let $g(u)=\lambda\|u\|_1$. Its proximal operator is the soft-thresholding function:

$$ \boxed{ \left[\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(v)\right]_j = \operatorname{sign}(v_j) \max\left(|v_j|-\gamma\lambda,\,0\right). } $$

The convex conjugate of $g$ is

$$ g^*(q)= \begin{cases} 0, & \|q\|_\infty\leq\lambda,\\ +\infty, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$

Using Moreau's identity, its proximal operator becomes a projection:

$$ \boxed{ \left[\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}(q)\right]_j = \min\left(\lambda,\max(-\lambda,q_j)\right). } $$

The dual update is therefore

$$ \boxed{ Q^{k+1} = \operatorname{clip} \left( Q^k+\sigma D_2\overline{R}^{\,k}, -\lambda,\lambda \right). } $$

Answer 3.2(e).

The L1 proximal operator uses soft-thresholding, which encourages sparse second-order differences. Using Moreau's identity, the dual update becomes a simple clipping operation between −λ and λ.

f) Construct the $T −2 × T$ matrix of the discrete Laplacian $D_2$.
In [6]:
# Compute the second difference matrix
second_difference = second_difference_matrix(len(days))
print(f"D2 shape: {second_difference.shape}")
print(f"D2 spectral norm: {np.linalg.norm(second_difference.toarray(), 2):.6f}")

D2 shape: (68, 70)
D2 spectral norm: 3.997945
D2 spectral norm: 3.997945

The second-order difference operator is defined by

$$ (D_2R)_t = R_t - 2R_{t+1} + R_{t+2}, \qquad t=1,\ldots,T-2. $$

Its matrix representation is

$$ \boxed{ D_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0\\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 1 & \cdots & 0\\ \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots\\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{(T-2)\times T}. } $$

Answer 3.2(f).

The matrix has shape (68, 70), with each row computing a second-order difference across three consecutive days. Its spectral norm is approximately 3.997945, which will be used to select suitable step sizes for the primal–dual algorithm.

g) Show that by setting $\tilde{\mathbf{Z}} := \mathbf{Z}/\alpha$ for some $\alpha>0$, $$D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\tilde{\mathbf{Z}} \,\middle\|\, \mathbf{R}^{[k]} \odot \Phi^{\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}}\right) = \frac{1}{\alpha} D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\mathbf{Z} \,\middle\|\, \mathbf{R}^{[k]} \odot \Phi^{\mathbf{Z}}\right).$$

Justify that running Algorithm 1 with

  • $\mathbf{Z}$ and $\Phi^{\mathbf{Z}}$ as input with a given $\lambda$,
  • or with $\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}$ and $\Phi^{\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}}$ rescaled by a factor $\alpha=\operatorname{std}(\mathbf{Z})$ and rescaled regularization parameter $\tilde{\lambda}:=\lambda/\operatorname{std}(\mathbf{Z})$,

gives the same reproduction number estimate $\widehat{\mathbf{R}}$.
In [7]:
""" 
The normalization factor alpha is computed using the standard deviation of the observed infections.
ddof = 1 Use sample standard deviation
ddof = 0 Use population standard deviation
"""
alpha = np.std(observed_infections, ddof=1)
normalized_infections = observed_infections / alpha
normalized_infectiousness = infectiousness / alpha
print(f"alpha = {alpha:.4f}")

alpha = 121651.5966

We normalize the infection counts and infectiousness using

$$ \alpha=\operatorname{std}(Z)=121651.5966. $$

The normalized quantities are

$$ \boxed{ \widetilde{Z}=\frac{Z}{\alpha}, \qquad \widetilde{\Phi}^{Z}=\frac{\Phi^Z}{\alpha}, \qquad \widetilde{\lambda}=\frac{\lambda}{\alpha}. } $$

The KL divergence satisfies

$$ D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left( \widetilde{Z}\mid R\odot\widetilde{\Phi}^{Z} \right) = \frac{1}{\alpha} D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left( Z\mid R\odot\Phi^Z \right). $$

Answer 3.2(g).

We divide the infection counts, infectiousness and regularization parameter by the same factor. This rescales the objective without changing its minimizer and improves numerical stability.

h) Implement Algorithm 1 and run it on the data Z. Plot the estimated reproduction number R
and the evolution of the objective function $ k \mapsto D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\mathbf{Z} \,\middle\|\, \mathbf{R}^{[k]} \odot \Phi^{\mathbf{Z}}\right) + \lambda \left\|\mathbf{D}_2 \mathbf{R}^{[k]}\right\|_1 $
along iterations to illustrate convergence of the scheme.
In [8]:
# Compute L1 solutions for different values of lambda
lambda_values = (0.5, 3.5, 15, 50, 150, 250)
affine_reproduction, affine_dual, affine_threshold = affine_start(
    normalized_infections, normalized_infectiousness, second_difference)

l1_solutions = {}
previous_solution = None

for lambda_value in lambda_values:
    use_affine = lambda_value >= affine_threshold
    solution = estimate_reproduction_number(
        normalized_infections, normalized_infectiousness, lambda_value, second_difference,
        initial_reproduction=affine_reproduction if use_affine else (
            None if previous_solution is None else previous_solution.reproduction_number),
        initial_dual=affine_dual if use_affine else (
            None if previous_solution is None else previous_solution.dual_variable))
    l1_solutions[lambda_value] = solution
    previous_solution = solution
    print(f"lambda={lambda_value:g}, objective={solution.final_objective:.5f}, "
          f"iterations={solution.iterations}, converged={solution.converged}")

3.3 — Tikhonov penalization

a) From Exercise 2, deduce the proximity operator of $x \mapsto \|x\|_2^2.$

Let $g(u)=\|u\|_2^2$. Its proximal operator is defined by

$$ \operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(v) = \underset{u}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left\{ \frac{1}{2}\|u-v\|_2^2+\gamma\|u\|_2^2 \right\}. $$

Setting the gradient to zero gives

$$ u-v+2\gamma u=0. $$

Therefore,

$$ \boxed{ \operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(v) = \frac{v}{1+2\gamma}. } $$

Answer 3.3(a).

The squared L2 norm has a simple proximal operator obtained by setting the gradient to zero. Each component is divided by the same positive factor, which smoothly reduces its magnitude.

b) Replace the $\ell_1$ penalization, $\|\mathbf{D}_2\mathbf{R}\|_1$, by a squared $\ell_2$ penalization $\|\mathbf{D}_2\mathbf{R}\|_2^2$, also called Tikhonov regularization. Implement Algorithm 1 replacing $\|\cdot\|_1$ by $\|\cdot\|_2^2$.
Indication: the convergence condition does not change.

We replace the L1 penalty with the Tikhonov penalty:

$$ \boxed{ \widehat{R} = \underset{R\geq 0}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left\{ D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z\mid R\odot\Phi^Z) + \lambda\|D_2R\|_2^2 \right\}. } $$

For $g(u)=\lambda\|u\|_2^2$, the convex conjugate is

$$ g^*(q)=\frac{\|q\|_2^2}{4\lambda}. $$

The dual update therefore becomes

$$ \boxed{ Q^{k+1} = \frac{ Q^k+\sigma D_2\overline{R}^{\,k} }{ 1+\dfrac{\sigma}{2\lambda} }. } $$

The primal update remains unchanged:

$$ R^{k+1} = \operatorname{prox}_{\tau F} \left(R^k-\tau D_2^\top Q^{k+1}\right), $$

where $F(R)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Z\mid R\odot\Phi^Z)$.

The convergence condition is

$$ \boxed{ \tau\sigma\|D_2\|_2^2<1, \qquad \|D_2\|_2\approx3.997945. } $$

Answer 3.3(b).

We replace the L1 dual clipping step with a simple scaling operation. The primal update and step-size condition remain unchanged because the operator D2 is the same.

c) Plot the two estimates on the same graph and comment.

Indication: the optimal parameter $\lambda$, i.e., the one for which the estimate is regular
while still reflecting the pandemic dynamics, might change depending on whether the $\ell_1$ or $\ell_2^2$ penalization is used.
In [12]:
# Compare the L1 solution with Tikhonov regularization
comparison_lambda = 3.5
tikhonov_solution = estimate_reproduction_number(
    normalized_infections, normalized_infectiousness, comparison_lambda,
    second_difference, penalty="tikhonov",
    initial_reproduction=l1_solutions[comparison_lambda].reproduction_number)

print(f"Tikhonov converged: {tikhonov_solution.converged}")
plt.plot(days, l1_solutions[comparison_lambda].reproduction_number, label="L1")
plt.plot(days, tikhonov_solution.reproduction_number, label="Tikhonov")
plt.xlabel("Day")
plt.ylabel("Reproduction number")

plt.savefig("figures/Figure_07_L1_versus_Tikhonov.png", dpi=200, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

The L1 estimate follows a clear piecewise-linear trend, while the converged Tikhonov estimate retains more local fluctuations. Both methods reduce the noise seen in the MLE, but their regularization parameters should be tuned separately for a fair comparison.

ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS¶

(a) Data fidelity Vs L1 regularity¶

For each tested regularization weight, we represent the two terms of the same normalized objective separately:

$$F_{\mathrm{KL}}(R)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\widetilde Z\mid R\odot\widetilde\Phi^Z), \qquad J_1(R)=\|D_2R\|_1.$$

The diagram reveals the price paid in data fidelity when imposing stronger smoothness. The curve is a trade-off visualization, not a proof that one $\lambda$ is optimal. The results at $\lambda=150$ and $250$ can overlap because the affine solution has already been reached.

In [13]:
# ADDITIONAL / OPTIONAL Figure 8: diagnostics computed from the six converged L1 solutions.
tradeoff = plot_fidelity_regularity(
    l1_solutions,

lambda=  250 | KL=10.34779 | ||D2 R||_1=0.00000

Interpretation.

Increasing $\lambda$ reduces the total second-order variation $\|D_2R\|_1$ but generally increases the KL data-fitting loss. Hence lower roughness is not automatically better estimation: the choice of $\lambda$ expresses a scientific compromise. In this dataset, the larger tested weights converge to approximately the same affine regime.

(b) What L1 & Tikhonov penalize¶

$$D_2\widehat R_{\ell_1}\quad\text{and}\quad D_2\widehat R_{\mathrm{Tikhonov}}.$$

Both curves were computed at the previously used nominal $\lambda=3.5$. Since $\lambda\|D_2R\|_1$ and $\lambda\|D_2R\|_2^2$ have different scales, equal numerical weights do not imply equal regularization strength.

L1:       ||D2 R||_1=0.08841; ||D2 R||_2^2=0.00272
Tikhonov: ||D2 R||_1=2.42866; ||D2 R||_2^2=0.16519

Interpretation.

The L1 penalty promotes a sparse second-difference signal, corresponding to long nearly affine intervals separated by localized changes in slope. The squared-L2 penalty distributes curvature more continuously. The figure illustrates the structural difference between the two penalties, not an unconditional claim that one method is statistically superior.

Conclusion

The Maximum Likelihood Estimator showed large daily fluctuations, ranging from 0.0114 to 2.1355. L1 regularization gave a smoother, piecewise-linear estimate, while Tikhonov regularization kept more short-term variations.

The primal–dual algorithm met the convergence criterion for all six tested L1 parameters (λ = 0.5, 3.5, 15, 50, 150, and 250), as well as for Tikhonov regularization. At λ = 150 and 250, the L1 estimates became nearly straight lines, showing that too much regularization can hide changes in transmission.

Overall, the results show why regularization is useful, but also why its strength must be chosen carefully.
